title: The tools running your store are now the tools running these lawsuits.
summary: If you run an ecommerce site, the tools you use every day, like ad pixels, session replay, chat widgets, even your search bar, are the same tools fueling a wave of lawsuits in California right now.
body_text: The tools running your store are now the tools running these lawsuits. The California Assembly's Committee on Privacy and Consumer Protection is holding a hearing on SB 690 , a bill meant to slow the flood of opportunistic litigation against online businesses under the California Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA). A Cold War wiretapping law, pointed at your checkout page Quick background, in case you've been lucky enough to avoid this one so far: CIPA is a Cold War–era criminal statute written to stop the wiretapping of landline phones. Plaintiffs' attorneys dusted it off, pointed it at ordinary web technologies, and argued that it applies to features like pixels, session replay, and search bars. It carries a private right of action and a $5,000 per-violation penalty. Thousands of cases have been filed in California. It's likely tens of thousands more have quietly settled. One federal judge put it bluntly: "The language of CIPA is a total mess. It was a mess from the get-go, but the mess gets bigger and bigger as the world continues to change… it is imperative for the Legislature to bring CIPA into the modern age." What SB 690 tries to fix SB 690 tries to do exactly that. It would exempt personal information processed for a "commercial business purpose," which is already covered under the CCPA. The Senate passed it unanimously in June 2025. It's been sitting in the Assembly ever since. Nobody installs a pixel thinking about a wiretapping law. Here's the part most ecommerce teams don't see coming. You probably didn't add any of these tools with a privacy statute in mind. A pixel went in for attribution. Session replay got installed to debug checkout. Chat showed up to cut support tickets. None of it felt like a legal decision at the time. That's usually how this kind of exposure builds, one tool at a time, until a statute like CIPA makes it visible. Here's hoping the hearing builds some momentum, because California could use a cleaner rulebook. In the meantime, it's worth knowing what's firing on your site and why.

title: 7 Automated Lead Generation Tools for Local Service Companies (2026)
summary: Compare 7 automated lead generation tools for local service businesses, with current 2026 pricing and an honest take on which fits HVAC, cleaning, and landscaping companies.
body_text: If you run an HVAC, landscaping, cleaning, or other local service business, your next customer is almost always searching online right now. The hard part is being the one they find and reply to before a competitor does. Automated lead generation tools handle the repetitive work of finding prospects, reaching out, and following up, so a steady flow of jobs does not depend on you remembering to chase every lead by hand. This guide compares 7 tools that local service companies actually use, with current 2026 pricing and an honest take on who each one fits. Prices change often, so treat these as starting points and confirm on each vendor's site before you buy. The 7 tools at a glance: Cohesive AI : Built for local service outbound. Pulls local business data and runs AI cold email campaigns. Custom pricing based on your needs. HubSpot : Broad CRM with marketing, sales, and service tools. Starter from $15/month per seat on annual billing. LeadSquared : Mobile CRM with strong field sales features. From about $25/user/month on annual billing. ActiveCampaign : Email and marketing automation with a deep workflow builder. Starter from $15/month for 1,000 contacts. Pipedrive : Sales-focused CRM with an easy pipeline. Lite from $14/user/month, with the LeadBooster add-on at $32.50/month. Thumbtack Pro : Pay-per-lead marketplace that connects you with local jobs. No monthly subscription. Keap : All-in-one CRM, automation, and invoicing for established small businesses. From $249/month on annual billing. Quick Comparison : Tool Starting Price (2026) Key Strength Best For Cohesive AI Custom Local data and AI cold email Local service outbound HubSpot $15/mo per seat All-around CRM and marketing Teams wanting one platform LeadSquared $25/user/mo Mobile and field sales Teams in the field ActiveCampaign $15/mo Email automation depth Nurture-heavy marketing Pipedrive $14/user/mo Simple sales pipeline Sales-led teams Thumbtack Pro Pay-per-lead No upfront commitment Trying paid leads fast Keap $249/mo CRM plus payments Established service firms The right pick depends on how you get customers today. If your growth depends on outbound, a tool built for finding and emailing local prospects matters most. If you mostly need to organize inbound leads and keep them warm, a CRM or email platform is the better starting point. Why Local Service Companies Need Automated Lead Generation Local service businesses face a few problems that automation is genuinely good at solving. Most people now find local services through online search, so being easy to find and quick to respond directly affects how many jobs you win. Manual outreach breaks down the moment you get busy with actual work, which is exactly when leads slip through the cracks. Smoothing out seasonal demand. HVAC and landscaping swing hard with the seasons. Automated outreach lets you fill slower months by reaching prospects steadily instead of scrambling only when the schedule is empty. Focusing on quality leads. Chasing every inquiry by hand wastes time on prospects who will never book. Automated tools help you spot who is actively looking, track who engages with your outreach, and prioritize the leads most likely to turn into paying jobs. Following up consistently. Most jobs are won in the follow-up, not the first message. Automation sends timely, consistent follow-ups so a slow reply does not cost you the work. What to Look for in a Lead Generation Tool When comparing options, weigh these against how your business actually operates: Local targeting. Can it find and reach prospects in your specific service area, not just generic contacts? Outreach automation. Does it handle cold email, follow-ups, and scheduling, or only store contacts you add yourself? Ease of use. A tool you never fully set up returns nothing. Simpler is often better for a small team. True total cost. Watch for setup fees, per-user pricing, and add-ons that change the real monthly number. Compliance. If you send cold email, the tool should help you stay within email and anti-spam rules. Cohesive AI Cohesive AI is built specifically for local service outbound. It pulls local business data and runs AI-assisted cold email campaigns aimed at the kinds of prospects HVAC, cleaning, and landscaping companies want to reach. The focus is narrow on purpose: instead of being a general CRM, it concentrates on finding local prospects and starting conversations with them. Pricing: Custom, based on your company's size and needs. Reach out for a quote. Best for: Local service businesses that want outbound lead generation handled for them rather than building it from scratch in a general-purpose CRM. HubSpot HubSpot is one of the most established CRM platforms, combining contact management, email marketing, and reporting in one place. Its Starter tier is priced at $20 per seat per month month-to-month, or $15 per seat per month on an annual commitment. The free tier is genuinely usable for getting organized, though the most valuable automation features sit in higher paid tiers. Pricing: Starter from $15/month per seat (annual). Free plan available with limits. Best for: Teams that want one broad platform for CRM, marketing, and service and are willing to grow into the higher tiers. LeadSquared LeadSquared stands out for mobile and field sales. Its pricing starts at $25 per user per month billed annually. If your team spends the day visiting job sites, the mobile CRM and field tracking are the draw. It is more sales-management software than outbound prospecting, so it fits teams that already have lead flow and need to manage it. Pricing: From about $25/user/month (annual). Implementation costs can add up, so confirm the full quote. Best for: Service businesses with reps in the field who need a strong mobile CRM. ActiveCampaign ActiveCampaign is known for one of the deeper automation builders in email marketing. The Starter plan begins at $15 per month for 1,000 contacts on annual billing, and plans scale up to Enterprise at $145 per month. Note that pricing rises with your contact count, so a growing list increases the bill. It shines at nurturing leads you already have rather than sourcing new local prospects. Pricing: Starter from $15/month for 1,000 contacts; scales with list size. Best for: Businesses that want sophisticated email nurture sequences and behavior-based workflows. Pipedrive Pipedrive is a clean, sales-focused CRM that most teams find easy to learn. Its Lite plan starts at $14 per user per month on annual billing. For lead capture specifically, the LeadBooster add-on starts at $32.50 per month per company and bundles a chatbot, live chat, web forms, and a prospecting database. Budget for those add-ons, since the base plan is mostly pipeline tracking. Pricing: Lite from $14/user/month (annual); LeadBooster add-on $32.50/month. Best for: Sales-led teams that want a simple, visual pipeline and will add lead capture on top. Thumbtack Pro Thumbtack Pro works differently from the others. Instead of a subscription, you pay per lead through a marketplace where local customers post jobs. There is no monthly software fee, which makes it a low-commitment way to test paid leads. The tradeoff is less control: you are competing with other pros on the platform, and lead quality varies. Pricing: Pay-per-lead, no subscription. Best for: Businesses that want to try paid local leads quickly without committing to software. Keap Keap (formerly Infusionsoft) bundles CRM, automation, email, invoicing, and appointment scheduling into one platform. It now runs on a single plan starting at $249 per month on annual billing, or $299 per month month-to-month, including two user licenses. A required onboarding fee adds upfront cost. It is a premium, all-in-one option rather than a budget pick. Pricing: From $249/month (annual). Onboarding fee applies. Best for: Established service businesses that want CRM, marketing, and payments in one tool and will use the full feature set. How to Choose Start with how you actually get customers, then match the tool to it: Need outbound prospecting? A tool built to find and email local prospects (like Cohesive AI) does the sourcing work general CRMs leave to you. Have leads but no system? A CRM like Pipedrive or HubSpot organizes them and keeps follow-ups on track. Want to nurture a list over time? ActiveCampaign's automation depth is hard to beat. Just want to test paid leads? Thumbtack Pro lets you try without a subscription. Want everything in one place? Keap covers CRM through invoicing for businesses ready for it. Most teams do best starting with one tool that fits their biggest current gap, rather than buying a broad suite they will only half use. Take advantage of free trials before committing, and recheck pricing on each vendor's site, since these numbers shift. Frequently Asked Questions What is the cheapest way to start with automated lead generation? Several tools start around $14 to $15 per month, including Pipedrive, ActiveCampaign, and HubSpot's Starter tier. Thumbtack Pro has no subscription at all, so you only pay for leads. The cheapest option that actually fits your workflow beats the cheapest option overall. Do I need a CRM and a lead generation tool, or just one? It depends on your gap. If you struggle to find new prospects, prioritize a lead generation or outbound tool. If you already get inquiries but lose track of them, a CRM matters more. Some businesses eventually use both, but starting with one is usually smarter. How do these tools handle seasonal demand? Automated outreach and follow-up let you reach prospects steadily year-round, so you can fill slower months by staying in front of leads instead of only marketing when work dries up.

title: Enterprise Asset Management for Skilled Nursing Chains
summary: Why nursing-home chains searching for enterprise asset management rarely need an industrial EAM suite, and what SNF-native asset management delivers instead across every building.
body_text: If you operate a chain of skilled nursing facilities and you have been searching for "enterprise asset management," you have probably landed on IBM Maximo, Infor EAM, SAP, or Hexagon. These are the category leaders, and they are serious software. They are also, for a nursing-home portfolio, almost always the wrong tool. Not because they are bad, but because they were built for a different building, a different budget, and a different problem. This guide is an honest map of that gap: what enterprise asset management actually is, who it is for, and why a chain should buy something else. The short version is that you do not need an industrial EAM platform. You need vertical, SNF-native asset management, and that is a category worth naming clearly. The reason to get this right is money. A typical 110-bed skilled nursing facility loses $155,000 to $500,000 a year to equipment waste: rentals that keep billing past their return date, owned wheelchairs nobody can find, duplicate purchases sitting in a closet one floor up. The median skilled nursing facility runs on a 1.8 percent operating margin , so that waste can equal most of a single building's annual profit, repeated across every facility you hold. We break the full model down in the 2026 SNF equipment waste report . Any system you evaluate has to move that number. What enterprise asset management actually is Enterprise asset management is the practice, and the software category, for managing the maintenance of physical assets across their entire lifecycle: acquisition, installation, operation, maintenance, and disposal. A full EAM suite handles preventive-maintenance scheduling, work-order management, reliability and condition monitoring, spare-parts and materials inventory, warranty tracking, depreciation, and capital planning across many sites at once. It evolved as an extension of the CMMS (the maintenance work-order tool) into something broader and more strategic. The leaders are genuinely industrial-grade. IBM Maximo is the category standard for global, asset-intensive deployments, layering AI and IoT-driven predictive maintenance across manufacturing, energy, and transportation. SAP EAM is the choice when an organization is already standardized on SAP S/4HANA, so asset maintenance ties into finance and procurement. Hexagon EAM dominates mining and utilities; Infor EAM serves the mid-market with lower overhead than the Tier 1 platforms. Who buys this? Asset-intensive enterprises: utilities, oil and gas, manufacturing plants, mining, transportation fleets, and large hospital systems managing thousands of medical devices, depreciation schedules, and compliance across a network. If you own turbines, production lines, or a biomed department running a device fleet the size of a small city, EAM earns its keep. That is a real job, and these are the right tools for it. Why industrial EAM is the wrong shape for a nursing-home chain The problem is not capability. It is fit, and it shows up in three places. It is heavy. An EAM implementation is often a bigger IT project than the software license itself. Enterprise Maximo and SAP EAM rollouts commonly run 12 to 24 months, and mid-market operations regularly end up with deployments that take three years, cost millions, and deliver functionality a leaner tool would have provided in months. Per-user fees typically start north of $100 a month before the seven-figure implementation. That is a capital project with a dedicated project team. A 1.8 percent-margin SNF chain does not have the budget, the IT department, or the appetite for a three-year install multiplied across twenty buildings. It is generic. EAM is built to manage any physical asset in any industry, which is its strength and, for skilled nursing, its weakness. It does not carry the specific workflows a nursing home lives on: rental elimination, cross-facility equipment sharing, and survey-ready audit reports keyed to skilled nursing's F-tags. You would be configuring a general-purpose industrial platform to approximate a job a purpose-built tool does out of the box. We lay out why generic asset tools struggle in this setting in why skilled nursing should not use general asset software . It does not track physical location automatically. This is the big one. Core EAM records an asset's location as a data field someone updates, not as continuous physical position. To get live indoor location you bolt on a separate real-time location system, which is a second capital install. On a nursing floor where a wheelchair changes rooms several times a week and nurses already lose 30 to 60 minutes a shift hunting for equipment, a location field that only updates when someone remembers to update it drifts from reality within weeks. And the single largest equipment leak in skilled nursing, rentals that should have gone back, is invisible unless you know the live location and status of every billable item without asking anyone to do anything. What a skilled nursing portfolio actually needs Strip the problem down and a nursing-home chain needs five things, none of which require an industrial EAM suite: Room-level equipment location, automatically — which room the item is in, always current, with no staff scanning. Rental elimination — catch every rental still billing after the resident stopped needing it, because that is where the biggest, most repeatable dollars hide. Cross-facility sharing — move idle equipment from one building to another instead of renting a second unit, the structural advantage only a multi-facility owner has. Survey readiness — produce a live, room-level equipment picture on demand, since F689, the accident-and-hazards tag under 42 CFR Part 483 , is the most-cited F-tag in the country. Standardization — one workflow and one price shape across every building, so every administrator runs the same playbook and the portfolio reports the same way. That is enterprise asset management too. It is just vertical, purpose-built for skilled nursing rather than for a refinery. Norra: enterprise asset management, purpose-built for skilled nursing Norra is the AI equipment manager for skilled nursing, and it delivers exactly those five things. Proprietary smart tags with multi-year battery life report room-level location through plug-in gateways, so staff never scan anything and the map stays current on its own. There is no wiring, no infrastructure buildout, and no six-figure install. It is an operating expense, not a capital project, at a fraction of the cost of a traditional enterprise system, and each building normally goes live in days. Norra is a MatrixCare marketplace partner with a live integration, works alongside any EHR, is HIPAA-compliant, and tracks equipment, not residents. Across a multi-facility skilled nursing network, Norra cut equipment spending by as much as 70 percent, drove 90 percent fewer new rental orders per month, saved over 1,100 staff hours a year, and brought unnecessary rentals to zero. Those are the numbers a chain operator can underwrite across a whole holding. For the wider portfolio case, see the best equipment tracking for PE-owned SNF portfolios , and for the Infor-specific comparison, Norra vs Infor location intelligence for SNF chains . Industrial EAM vs Norra, side by side Capability Norra Industrial EAM (Maximo, Infor, SAP) Automatic room-level DME location ✅ Always current, no scanning ❌ Manual location field or bolt-on RTLS Staff scanning required ✅ None, fully automatic ❌ Manual record updates Full asset-lifecycle and maintenance management Equipment location and spend lifecycle for DME ✅ Industrial-grade, procure to disposal Preventive maintenance and work orders Equipment status logs, not a full CMMS ✅ Core strength Reliability and predictive maintenance (IoT) Not the focus ✅ Mature capability Built for skilled nursing DME ✅ Purpose-built ❌ Generic across industries Rental-elimination workflow ✅ Built in ❌ Not a rental or location tool Cross-facility sharing across a chain ✅ Built in ⚠️ Via enterprise configuration Survey-ready audit reports ✅ One click ❌ Not survey-shaped Implementation Live in days, no capital project 12 to 24 months, seven-figure install Pricing model Operating expense, no upfront cost Large upfront license and implementation (CapEx) Read the concessions honestly. Industrial EAM genuinely wins on full-lifecycle maintenance, work-order management, and reliability engineering across asset-intensive industries. That is what it is for, it does it well, and Norra is not a maintenance suite. Norra wins on the things that decide whether a nursing-home chain keeps its money: automatic room-level location with zero scanning, rental elimination, cross-facility sharing, survey readiness, and a price shaped like an SNF operating budget that standardizes across every building. The bottom line Choose an industrial EAM suite if you manage thousands of fixed and mobile assets across an asset-intensive enterprise — utilities, manufacturing, transportation, or a large hospital system with a biomed department and a capital budget — and need reliability engineering and full maintenance-lifecycle planning. Choose Norra if you operate a skilled nursing facility or chain and want equipment waste gone and standardized: automatic room-level location with no scanning, rental elimination, cross-facility sharing, and survey-ready reports, live in days across every building with no upfront cost. A nursing-home portfolio searching for "enterprise asset management" is rarely searching for Maximo. It is searching for control over its equipment, building by building, without a three-year install. That is enterprise asset management purpose-built for skilled nursing, and it is what Norra was made to do. To see your portfolio's equipment on one live map, start with a single-facility pilot at norra.io .

title: DDoS-for-Hire and the Evolving Use of AI
body_text: Executive Summary Since our seven-part analysis of the DDoS-for-hire landscape in December 2024, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the booter/stresser ecosystem has accelerated significantly. What was then an emerging trend has now become an operational reality across multiple stages of the attack lifecycle. This update examines developments through Q4 2025, focusing on three key areas: the proliferation of malicious large language models (LLMs) purpose-built for offensive operations, AI-generated tools explicitly designed for botnet recruitment, and the measurable impact on attack volume and sophistication. These developments represent a fundamental shift in how DDoS-for-hire services operate and who can access them. Key Takeaways Malicious LLMs now offer tiered access: From free tools (KawaiiGPT) to premium platforms (Xanthorox), AI-assisted attack development is available at every price point. AI is accelerating botnet recruitment: The KuroCracks scanner demonstrates explicit use of ChatGPT to optimize exploitation tools for botnet growth. Underground AI adoption is quantifiable: 219 percent increase in malicious AI tool mentions, 52 percent increase in jailbreaking discussions. Attack metrics reflect expanded threat actor population: Consistent acceleration in attack volume and sophistication across vendor reports. Evasion is evolving: AI-powered traffic mimicry and adaptive attack patterns challenge signature-based detection. Law enforcement faces a resilience problem: AI enables rapid reconstitution of seized infrastructure. The Malicious LLM Ecosystem Matures The underground market for malicious AI tools has evolved beyond simple jailbreaks of commercial models such as ChatGPT. Threat actors now have access to purpose-built platforms designed specifically for offensive cyber operations, with DDoS tool development among their advertised capabilities. The implication for distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) operations is clear: The time from “idea” to “weaponized script” continues to compress. GhostGPT: Purpose-Built for Speed In January 2025, Abnormal Security documented GhostGPT , a Telegram-distributed malicious chatbot marketed for rapid exploit development. Priced at just $50/week , GhostGPT specifically advertises malware creation and exploit code generation with no ethical guardrails. Unlike Xanthorox’s complex modular architecture, GhostGPT prioritizes accessibility and speed, with users reporting functional attack scripts within minutes of initial prompts. WormGPT Resurfaces with New Variants Despite the original WormGPT developer’s announcement that they were shutting down operations in 2023, the tool has proven resilient. Unit 42 researchers documented WormGPT 4 advertisements appearing on Telegram channels in late September 2025, with subscriber counts exceeding 500 users. CATO Networks separately identified new WormGPT variants built on open-source foundations, including Mixtral and xAI’s Grok models. Analysis from Moxso confirms that WormGPT retains capabilities directly relevant to DDoS operations, including the ability to generate “malicious code designed to take down websites and infrastructure by overloading them with traffic.” The pricing model remains accessible: $50 per month/$175 annually/$220 lifetime , placing sophisticated script generation within reach of virtually any threat actor. Xanthorox AI: A Modular Offensive Platform The most significant new entrant in 2025 is Xanthorox AI , which first appeared on Telegram in October of 2024 and then on darknet forums in late Q1 2025. Xanthorox operates as a modular platform with five specialized AI models spanning code generation, image analysis, social engineering content, voice interaction, and real-time reconnaissance via more than 50 search engines. The subscription model reportedly runs $300/month or $2,500 annually on dark web channels, positioning Xanthorox as an “enterprise-grade” offensive AI platform. Important caveat: Trend Micro’s technical review of Xanthorox identified significant limitations, including reliance on Google infrastructure and missing advertised features. As with many underground tools, marketing claims may exceed actual capabilities. However, even partially functional offensive AI tools lower barriers meaningfully. KawaiiGPT: Free and Accessible At the other end of the spectrum, Picus Security and Palo Alto’s Unit 42 documented KawaiiGPT , an anime-themed malicious LLM that “democratizes cybercrime by allowing any amateur to generate professional-grade attacks for free.” The July 2025 v2.5 release is available on GitHub, with setup taking less than five minutes. AI-Optimized Vulnerability Scanners for Botnet Recruitment Perhaps the most directly relevant development for DDoS infrastructure is the emergence of AI-assisted tools explicitly designed to accelerate botnet growth. However, it’s important to note that AI-enhanced vulnerability scanning is not exclusive to malicious actors; offensive security (offsec) professionals and penetration testers also leverage similar tools for white-hat purposes, such as identifying vulnerable devices before attackers can exploit them and helping organizations remediate weaknesses in their infrastructure. The KuroCracks Scanner S2W TALON’s threat intelligence documented a January 2025 post on the Cracked Forum by a threat actor using the handle “KuroCracks.” The post advertised an open-source scanner for CVE-2024-10914 (a remote code execution vulnerability) with the explicit title: CVE-2024-10914 SCANNER - REMOTE CODE EXECUTION - GREAT FOR BOTNETS - OPEN SOURCE The scanner combined Masscan automation with exploit delivery, but what makes it significant is that KuroCracks explicitly stated the tool was optimized using ChatGPT . The threat actor shared prompt engineering techniques used to elicit exploit code from AI models, providing a template for others to follow. This represents a concrete example of AI accelerating the vulnerability-to-botnet pipeline. Rather than manually developing exploitation tools, threat actors can now iterate rapidly using commercial LLMs, even when those models have guardrails in place. Separately, S2W TALON documented threat actors targeting LLM infrastructure itself, with one BreachForums user offering exploits for the Google Gemini API, indicating criminal communities view AI platforms as high-value targets. Underground AI Tool Adoption Accelerates Multiple threat intelligence providers have quantified the surge in underground AI activity. KELA’s Findings KELA’s 2025 AI Threat Report found the following: 219 percent increase in mentions of malicious AI tools and tactics on monitored dark web sources 52 percent increase in discussions specifically about jailbreaking legitimate AI tools The trajectory is notable: KELA tracked 4,167 mentions of jailbreaking techniques in 2024, up from 2,747 in 2023. Among the most frequently shared: “DAN” (Do Anything Now) prompts and techniques for bypassing content filters in ChatGPT and Gemini to generate network flooding scripts. This represents not just awareness, but active skill-building within criminal communities. Threat actors are systematically documenting and sharing techniques to extract DDoS-relevant code from commercial models, even when those models have guardrails in place. Flashpoint’s Analysis Flashpoint’s research , based on analysis of more than 2.5 million AI-related posts from more than 100,000 illicit sources, identified active communities sharing “bypass builders” that specialize in defeating ChatGPT and Gemini guardrails. The implication is clear: Even without access to purpose-built malicious LLMs, threat actors are actively developing techniques to weaponize commercial AI tools for offensive purposes, including DDoS attack development. The Measurable Impact: 2025 Attack Statistics Industrywide data confirms the acceleration. NETSCOUT’s ATLAS platform observed more than 8 million DDoS attacks globally in the first half of 2025 , with peak attacks reaching 3.12Tbps in bandwidth and 1.5Gpps in throughput. ENISA’s October 2025 Threat Landscape report found that DDoS accounted for 77 percent of all reported cyber incidents in the EU. These metrics reflect an expanded threat actor population enabled by lowered technical barriers. Although no single metric can be attributed solely to AI adoption, the consistent pattern of acceleration across vendors suggests that lowered barriers are expanding the threat actor population. The Acceleration Effect Unit 42’s incident response research demonstrated how AI compresses attack timelines. Researchers simulated a complete ransomware attack, from initial access to data exfiltration, in 25 minutes using AI assistance at every stage . This represents approximately a 100x speed increase over traditional methods. The same acceleration principles apply to DDoS operations: Reconnaissance that once took days can now be completed in minutes, and custom attack scripts can be generated on demand rather than developed over weeks. AI-Enhanced Evasion Techniques Beyond tool development, AI is increasingly applied to attack execution. Imperva’s 2025 Bad Bot Report notes that “AI is fueling bot attacks, making them more intelligent and more evasive than ever before.” The report found simple bot attacks increasing from 34 percent to 52 percent in the travel sector, “supporting the theory that AI is fueling a surge in simple bot activity” that overwhelms traditional defenses through sheer volume and variation. Capabilities now include automated traffic shaping to mimic legitimate users and dynamic parameter adjustment based on observed defensive responses. Law Enforcement Continues Pressure Law enforcement sustained pressure throughout 2025. Key enforcement actions that started in 2024 and continued into 2025 include: 2024: 27 domains seized, 18 booter services disrupted , including zdstresser.net, starkstresser.net, and orbitalstress.net; three administrators arrested, 300 users identified ( BleepingComputer ). May 2025: Nine domains seized and six DDoS-for-hire platforms disrupted ; Poland arrested four administrators of platforms, including Cfxapi, Cfxsecurity, neostress, jetstress, quickdown, and zapcut ( DOJ ). July 2025 ( Operation Eastwood ): Europol coordinated a 12-country operation targeting NoName057(16) , the pro-Russian hacktivist group. The operation disrupted more than 100 servers, issued seven international arrest warrants (six for Russian nationals), and made two arrests in France and Spain. Notably, authorities contacted more than 1,100 DDoSia contributors about potential criminal liability, a deterrence strategy aimed at the group’s crowd-sourced attack model ( Europol ). August 2025: DOJ charged a 22-year-old Oregon man for operating RapperBot , a botnet responsible for more than 370,000 DDoS attacks against 18,000 victims in more than 80 countries. The botnet controlled between 65,000 and 95,000 infected devices with an attack capacity of between 2 and 6 Tbps ( DOJ ). UK National Cyber Crime Unit’s Frank Tutty noted that “booter services are an attractive entry-level cybercrime, and users can go on to even more serious offending,” a trajectory that AI tools now accelerate. Conclusion: The Adaptive Imperative The developments documented here, from tiered malicious LLM access to AI-optimized botnet recruitment to accelerating attack volumes , represent the current state of AI integration into DDoS-for-hire operations. Every prediction in our earlier analysis has materialized: AI-enhanced attacks now analyze defensive responses in real time, attack scripts are generated on demand via natural language interfaces, and the barrier between intent and capability continues to collapse. When one platform is seized, the underlying tools, techniques, and customer base migrate to successors within days rather than months. For defenders, the trajectory demands equally intelligent capabilities deployed proactively. Static, signature-based defenses face an increasingly untenable position against adaptive, AI-enhanced attacks. Organizations must assume that the threat actor population will continue expanding, that attack sophistication will continue increasing, and that the window between vulnerability disclosure and weaponized exploitation will continue shrinking. The adaptive imperative is no longer theoretical; it’s operational.

title: Introducing the Giga CLI
summary: The Giga CLI puts the whole platform on the command line — agents, tickets, tests, KPIs, secrets, knowledge base, and deploys. Anything you can do in the console, you can now do from your terminal, a script, a CI job, or a coding agent.
body_text: Improving a production support agent usually means a lot of context switching: open the dashboard, find the conversation, figure out what went wrong, edit the config, push, wait for the sync, discover a broken reference, and start over. If you spend your day in a terminal, or your coding agent does, that loop is slower than it needs to be. Today we’re launching the Giga CLI. It’s a single tool, giga , that gives you the full Giga platform from the command line: agents, tickets, tests, KPIs, secrets, knowledge base, and deploys. Anything you can do in the console, you can now do from your terminal, a script, a CI job, or a coding agent. pip install giga-sdk giga login That’s the whole install. The package ships both the CLI and the Python SDK ( from giga import Agent ) from one wheel, so the tool you script with and the library you build with stay in lockstep.

title: In Q2, portfolios came roaring back
summary: This market brief looks back at how insurers and private wealth investors weathered H1 turbulence and assesses portfolio positioning for the quarters ahead.
body_text: July 9, 2026 By Matthew Vegari, Head of Research At the start of the year, the macro outlook for 2026 looked stable: the Fed had cut several times and landed at or near neutral policy territory; tariff-induced inflation was rolling over; the consumer remained disgruntled yet poised to keep spending; the labor market had cooled but not gone cold. At the end of February, turmoil in the Middle East threatened to upend that equilibrium. The US and Israel launched a military campaign against Iran, and the calculus for investors changed overnight. Brent crude surged more than 55%. Yields spiked and equities plummeted as markets braced for a full-blown energy shock and another bout of inflation following Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz. By the end of Q2, however, such anxieties were a distant memory: oil prices had come back into check, equities had notched one of the fastest recoveries in decades, and long rates had retreated from their highs, if not having quite returned to pre-conflict lows. Now in Q3, the fundamentals of the economy look much as they did at the start of the year, barring marginally higher energy prices (and perhaps a more exasperated consumer): the AI boom marches ahead, credit markets remain healthy, and the Fed, under new leadership, has held rates steady (for now). This market brief looks back at how insurers and private wealth investors weathered H1 turbulence and assesses portfolio positioning for the quarters ahead. Insurers: A familiar dip but a flatter recovery Insurers are ending H1 in the black, up 2.2% year to date on average, though the path was anything but smooth. The shape of returns should look familiar: a rally through February, a sharp dip as the Iran conflict broke out, and a steady climb back through Q2. It’s the same dip-and-recovery pattern that defined 2025’s Liberation Day selloff. The difference is pace: last year’s YTD returns through June sat closer to 4%. In fact, this year’s trajectory looks less like 2025’s banner year for portfolios and more like 2024—a year that also saw its share of rate-hike scares, growth wobbles, and inflation surprises.
